name: Igala

summary.text: The Igala live mainly in southern and eastern Kogi State, in the angle where the Niger and Benue rivers meet. Their historic capital is Idah, on the Niger, seat of the Attah Igala, ruler of the Igala Kingdom. Igala is also spoken in riverside communities downstream and across the Niger: Olumbanasa in Anambra West, Igga, Ojjor and Ogurugu in Enugu, Ebu in Delta, and Ilushi and Ifeku in Edo.

areas.note: A mixed LGA. The Bassa-Nge, Bassa-Komo and Ebira Koto also live here.
A mixed LGA, shared with Ebira communities.

Indigenous to the confluence: the Attah of Igala ceded land at Lokoja to the British in 1841, and the owner reports Igala fishermen living there at the time. Today a large Igala population lives alongside many other peoples; no published figures give the share.

Two of the LGA's ten wards (Olumbanasa 1 and 2) are the Igala speaking Olumbanasa communities. How large a share the Igala are is disputed: local accounts say most people in these communities are Igala, while Amali and Bieresnu-Nnabugwu (2023) describe a small Igala speaking group in an Igbo majority LGA.
Igala speaking communities make up three of the LGA's sixteen wards (Igga/Asaba, Ojjor, Ogurugu), about 20 percent of its people, according to Vanguard (2026).
The riverside Illushi ward (Ilushi, Uloshi land, and part of Ifeku). The rest of the LGA is Esan.
Most of the Ifeku island communities, on the Niger in the north of the LGA.
The Ebu kingdom, one of the LGA's towns. The rest of the LGA is Igbo (Anioma).
Wikipedia: the people of Apa are "predominantly Idoma and a few Igalas". Apa borders the Igala LGAs of Kogi. The Igala villages here are not yet named.
Igala is spoken in Ette; the rest of the LGA is Igbo.
Ifeku communities, according to the owner. The boundary data does not yet place a mapped Ifeku village here; check which villages lie in Etsako East.

communities.name: Ebu
communities.note: The LGA describes Ebu as Igala speaking people who migrated from Idah. Glottolog lists Ebu as a dialect of Igala. Point from the LGA's own coordinates.

history.text: Founded by Igala speaking people who migrated from Idah across the Niger. The masquerade known as the “Ebu Wonder” and the White Eagle are symbols of the Ebu kingdom.

communities.name: Ilushi (Uloshi)
communities.note: Speaks the Olu dialect of Igala; organised in nine clans after the Igala Mela of Idah. Village positions from GRID3 where they could be found.

history.text: Once part of the Igala Kingdom; the people still call their father Attah. Colonial and later boundary changes placed them in Edo State.

livelihoods.text: Fishing, farming and trade along the Niger, near the borders of Kogi, Anambra and Delta.

communities.name: Ifeku
communities.note: Eleven Ifeku communities lie along the Niger and the Aika river. By the GRID3 boundaries, the villages mapped so far fall in Etsako Central (Ala-Ifeku, Owa-Ifeku, Ifeku Uyi, Okpatawo, Allah-Ifeku I) and Esan South-East (Allah-Ifeku II, Ifeku Island, Okwoshimili); Vanguard (2024) says the same. The owner places Ifeku in Etsako East and Etsako Central; the Etsako East villages are not yet located.

history.text: A 1923 British intelligence report records people living on Ifeku Island since before 1787.

livelihoods.text: Farming and fishing on fertile land by the Niger and Aika rivers; the island is now promoted for tourism.

communities.name: Olumbanasa
communities.note: Vanguard (2015) names seven Igala speaking communities, together called Olumbanasaa: Ode, Igbedor, Odekpe, Alla, Onugwa, Odomagwu and Igbokaenyi. Igbokenyi is an island on the Niger. Odomagwu could not be located yet.

history.text: Long among Anambra’s most neglected communities: in 2015 Vanguard described Igbokenyi, an island in the Niger with fewer than 2,000 people, as lacking water, electricity, roads and schools.

communities.name: Inoma and Owelle
communities.note: Listed as Igala towns by a 2024 post and by the owner, and inside the Olumbanasa 1 ward in GRID3, but not named in the Vanguard list. Ukwala could not be located yet.

livelihoods.text: Owelle Central market is one of the main markets of Anambra West.

communities.name: Nzam
communities.note: The LGA headquarters. The Nigerian Tribune (2021) calls Nzam an Igala speaking community, whose people protested marginalisation "in their ancestral land". Residents speak Igala and Igbo. One local history site (Nnewi City, 2025) describes Nzam as Igbo by identity with strong Igala ties.

history.text: The headquarters of Anambra West. In 2021 its Igala speaking people protested their marginalisation “in their ancestral land”.

livelihoods.text: A riverine town where most people farm or fish, growing yam, cassava, maize and rice.

communities.name: Ogurugu
communities.note: Daily Trust (2022) calls it a community where Igala is still widely spoken. The geolinguistic survey (2018) names it too.

history.text: Founded by Igala from Idah centuries ago. Its legendary figure Onoja Oboni is credited with building the old walls still visible today; a yearly festival is held at his grave, which women may not enter.

livelihoods.text: Fishing and river trade with Kogi across the Imabolo, and rice and yam farming.

history.text: One of the riverbank Igala communities of Enugu founded from Idah. Enugu’s Igala rulers receive their staff of office from the Attah at Idah.

livelihoods.text: Fishing and trade across the river with Kogi.

communities.name: Asaba (Uzo-Uwani)
communities.note: Not the Delta State capital. Part of the Igala speaking Igga/Asaba ward.

history.text: Faces the Igala communities of Kogi across the Imaboro river. Its ruler: “Igala is our mother tongue, but we are from Enugu State.”

livelihoods.text: Fishing and trade across the river with Kogi.

communities.name: Ette (Etteh)
communities.note: The Ette speak Idoma, Igala and Igbo. Egenti (2015) finds Idoma the strongest, then Igala, then Igbo; the owner reports Igala as a main language of Ette.

history.text: One of the two towns that make up Igbo-Eze North (with Enugu-Ezike), on the border with Benue. The Igala of the Nsukka area trace their arrival from Idah to the 17th century.

reviewNotes: The Kogi LGA list is now confirmed by Omachonu and Dalhatu (2018), which lists Igala in nine Kogi LGAs (including Bassa) and notes it is also spoken in Ajaokuta and Lokoja.

Not yet mapped, needs a source that Igala is SPOKEN there today (not only an origin tradition): Toto and Doma LGAs in Nasarawa (Umaisha, Panda). In Benue, Apa is now mapped as a minority area; the Benue towns in Kogi Reports (Otukpo, Otukpa, Agila, Ajomachi, Alifati) are Idoma speaking, and the Igala living in Makurdi (Daily Trust, 2026) are town residents rather than a distinct community, so neither is on the map.

Kogi Reports (2019) also lists many places with Igala origin traditions (for example Illah, Okpanam and Asaba in Delta, Agenebode and Anegbette in Edo, Nsukka towns in Enugu, Wukari, Ibadan). These are origin claims, not Igala speaking communities, so they are not on the map.
Odomagwu (Olumbanasa) and Ukwala (Anambra West) could not be located in GRID3 or OpenStreetMap.
Vanguard (2024) counts eleven Ifeku communities; only seven are located.
Igala speaking towns inside the mixed Kogi LGAs (Bassa, Ajaokuta, Lokoja) are not yet mapped as points.
Boston 1968 and Negedu 2014 are cited through Wikipedia and have not been checked directly.

Ogbadibo (Benue): asked about by the owner. Sources describe it as Idoma speaking, with Igala origin traditions (Owukpa founded from Ankpa); no source yet names an Igala speaking village there, so it is not on the Igala map. Add it if a source or the owner names such villages.
Umuebu (Ukwuani, Delta): Wikipedia’s Anioma article names an Igala minority there, but the owner reports Umuebu no longer speaks Igala; it is not mapped as an Igala speaking community.
